title: A Shut Strait of Hormuz Is Turning an Oil Shock Into a Structural Supply Crisis
summary: Brent crude has pushed back above $90 a barrel as the Strait of Hormuz, the chokepoint for roughly a fifth of the world's oil flows, remains effectively closed to commercial tankers. What matters here is not the weekly price move but the shift in how markets are reading the disruption: from a temporary flashpoint that would resolve itself to an open-ended, structural loss of Gulf supply that could persist well into next year.
context:
- A June 2026 memorandum of understanding between Washington and Tehran to reopen Hormuz to commercial shipping collapsed within weeks after disputes over which routes tankers could use, triggering renewed Iranian attacks on tankers and a reimposed US naval blockade.

- Traffic through the strait, which normally carries around a fifth of global oil consumption, has collapsed from roughly 130 daily transits before the conflict to as few as eight to fifteen, a scale of disruption far beyond typical Middle East risk premia priced into oil.

- The US Energy Information Administration does not expect Middle East oil production to return to pre-conflict levels until early 2027, reframing the episode as a multi-quarter supply event rather than a short-lived spike that fades once headlines move on.

- Washington has layered an economic campaign on top of military pressure, with Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent repeating threats of the "toughest sanctions in history" against Iran and any country continuing to buy its oil, adding a second, harder-to-price source of supply uncertainty.

- Because the disruption is structural rather than a single shock, it is feeding through into broader inflation expectations and energy-sector earnings simultaneously, rather than producing the sharp spike-and-reversal pattern markets are used to from past Gulf tensions.

title: Long-Dated Treasury Yields Hit a 19-Year High as Fiscal Strain Resurfaces
summary: The 30-year US Treasury yield pushed above 5.3%, its highest level since 2007, as investors demanded greater compensation for funding an ever-larger government borrowing programme. The move matters well beyond bond desks because it raises the cost of capital across mortgages, corporate debt and public financing all at once, and reflects a slow-building erosion of confidence in the sustainability of US fiscal policy rather than a single data point or headline.
context:
- Persistent US budget deficits mean the Treasury has to issue an increasing volume of long-dated debt; more supply requires higher yields to clear the market, a dynamic that has been building steadily through 2026 rather than emerging suddenly this week.

- Inflation has stayed above the Federal Reserve's 2% target for five consecutive years, with tariffs on imported goods and rising energy costs, compounded by the Hormuz disruption, keeping price pressures alive well past the point policymakers had expected them to fade.

- Yields have now held above 5% for the longest continuous stretch since before the 2008 financial crisis, a signal that investors increasingly see today's combination of deficits and inflation as durable rather than transitory.

- Higher long-term yields feed directly into mortgage rates and corporate borrowing costs, acting as a brake on rate-sensitive parts of the economy even as the Federal Reserve's short-term policy rate moves on a separate track.

- The sell-off has revived a longer-running debate about "fiscal dominance": the risk that government financing needs increasingly constrain the Fed's room to set monetary policy independently of the deficit, a concern that tends to compound rather than resolve quickly.

title: Corporate Earnings Are Booming, but the Growth Is Narrowly Concentrated
summary: With most S&P 500 companies now having reported second-quarter results, aggregate earnings growth has accelerated to its fastest pace since 2021. The headline figure matters less than its composition: much of the acceleration traces back to a handful of technology companies' artificial-intelligence spending and to a repricing of energy earnings, raising the question of how broad-based the underlying economy actually is beneath a very strong index-level number.
context:
- Alphabet, Amazon, Meta and Microsoft are together on pace to spend roughly $725 billion this year on AI infrastructure, and that capital spending is flowing directly into the earnings and margins of chipmakers, cloud providers and data-centre suppliers reporting this season.

- Analysts note the earnings beat is concentrated in the technology and energy sectors, driven respectively by the AI capex cycle and higher realised oil prices tied to the Hormuz disruption, rather than by broad-based strength across consumer, industrial or financial sectors.

- That concentration matters for market fragility: an index-level growth rate that looks robust can mask softer conditions elsewhere in the economy, and any slowdown in AI investment or reversal in energy prices could disproportionately hit reported earnings growth going forward.

- Retail sales fell for the first time in six months even as headline inflation held close to its recent range, an early sign that consumer spending outside AI-linked capital investment may be losing momentum beneath the strong corporate results.

- Investors are increasingly treating this earnings season as a test of whether AI infrastructure spending can keep generating adequate returns, given how much of aggregate profit growth now depends on the capital budgets of a small number of companies.
